title: Decidability of contractibility for finite two-dimensional complexes
formal: Is there an algorithm that, on every finite nonempty simplicial complex \(K\) of dimension at most two, halts and decides whether \(K\) is simple-homotopy equivalent to a point? Equivalently, can contractibility of all such \(K\) be decided?

context:
The source explicitly asks about deciding whether a two-dimensional complex admits a simple-homotopy equivalence to a point. Its separate parameterized problems bound expansions or ask to reach a graph; those are different computational tasks.

The source relates this decidability question to recognizing the trivial group from balanced finite presentations, which have the same number of defining relators and generators. Undecidability of the corresponding problem for arbitrary presentations cannot simply be transferred to this restriction. Likewise, a trivial fundamental group alone does not make every two-dimensional complex contractible.

The stable geometric Andrews–Curtis question asks whether every contractible two-dimensional complex can reach a point using moves of dimension at most three. Here the unknown is whether an algorithm can always decide contractibility, with higher-dimensional intermediate complexes allowed. The source recalls that dimension four already suffices when a contraction exists.

The 2023/2024 random simple-homotopy paper gives practical simplification methods and successful examples while explicitly retaining the open low-dimensional decidability question. A heuristic that finds reductions on many contractible inputs does not provide a halting, correct procedure for every input.
why: This is a basic boundary of algorithmic topology: whether a finite two-dimensional description admits any reliable procedure for recognizing a space with no nontrivial homotopy. It separates unrestricted computability from practical simplification and from resource-bounded versions of topological reduction.

Decide whether expansions and collapses can transform it into a single vertex.

definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite collection of nonempty finite vertex sets, called simplices, closed under taking nonempty subsets. A simplex with \(r+1\) vertices has dimension \(r\). The input explicitly lists its simplices, or equivalently its maximal simplices and their vertex labels. The promise is that every simplex has at most three vertices. Edges and triangles need not form a manifold or embed in Euclidean three-space.

An elementary collapse removes a pair \((\sigma,\tau)\) of simplices, where \(\sigma\) is a codimension-one face of \(\tau\) and the only simplex properly containing \(\sigma\) is \(\tau\). An elementary expansion is the inverse: add such a pair so that the result is again a simplicial complex and that pair could be collapsed immediately.

Simple-homotopy equivalence to a point means that a finite sequence of expansions and collapses takes \(K\) to a complex consisting of a single vertex. New vertices may be introduced; intermediate complexes may be larger and have dimension greater than two. There is no prescribed bound on the number of moves, number of vertices or intermediate dimension. Relabeling vertices has no mathematical effect.

For comparison with the topological formulation, the geometric realization \(|K|\) is obtained by gluing an ordinary Euclidean simplex for each face along its common subfaces. It is contractible if its identity map can be continuously deformed to a constant map: there exist \(p\in|K|\) and a continuous
\[H:|K|\times[0,1]\longrightarrow |K|,\qquad H(x,0)=x,\quad H(x,1)=p.\]
For a finite complex, being contractible is equivalent to having the simple-homotopy type of a point, as recalled in the sources.

The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine acting on the finite encoding. It must give the correct yes/no answer and terminate on both contractible and noncontractible inputs. No polynomial-time or other running-time bound is required. There is no promise that \(K\) is already contractible or simply connected, and no contraction certificate is supplied.

This is specifically recognition of the simple-homotopy type of a point. The card does not ask to decide equivalence of an arbitrary pair of complexes. It also does not restrict allowed moves to collapses alone, or impose a fixed expansion budget.
answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a total decision algorithm for this input class, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A procedure that eventually finds a contraction on yes-instances but may run forever on no-instances is insufficient. A hardness theorem ruling out efficient algorithms does not establish undecidability.
